readerTitle: Eight is great: how Wells Fargo's sales goals built a scandal
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Wells Fargo 무단 계좌 개설 사건, 2011~2020) + 가상 적용 (냉난방 설비 서비스 회사)
insight: 같은 잘못이 여러 곳에서 반복되면 사람이 아니라 그 사람들이 일하는 구조(목표, 보상, 압박)가 원인이다. 사람을 바꿔도 구조가 그대로면 행동도 그대로다.
misconception: 부정을 저지른 직원을 해고하면 문제가 해결된다. 썩은 사과 몇 개만 골라내면 된다.

sources.text: CFPB, OCC, City of Los Angeles enforcement actions against Wells Fargo, September 8, 2016 ($185M in fines; ~1.5M deposit and ~565,000 credit card accounts possibly unauthorized; ~5,300 employees terminated)
Independent Directors of the Board of Wells Fargo & Company, Sales Practices Investigation Report (April 2017)
Wells Fargo press release on the expanded third-party account review (August 2017, up to 3.5M potentially unauthorized accounts)
U.S. Department of Justice press release, February 21, 2020 ($3 billion settlement with DOJ and SEC)
Federal Reserve Board press release, February 2, 2018 (asset cap on Wells Fargo)
Reckard, E. S. (December 2013). Los Angeles Times investigation of sales pressure at Wells Fargo branches
Wells Fargo annual reports ("Eight is great" cross-sell goal; branches called "stores")
Meadows, D. (2008). Thinking in Systems: A Primer

factChecks.note: 2016년 9월 벌금 합계 $185M(CFPB $100M, OCC $35M, LA시 $50M), 은행 자체 분석 기준 예금계좌 약 150만, 신용카드 약 56.5만 건, 2011~2016년 약 5,300명 해고. CFPB 동의명령 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
2017년 8월 확대 조사에서 최대 350만 건으로 추정치가 늘어난 점, 2020년 2월 DOJ·SEC와 $30억 합의를 보도자료로 확인하세요.
CEO John Stumpf는 2016년 10월 사임. 카드에는 이름 없이 "weeks later"로만 적었습니다. 지점 직원의 상품 판매 목표 폐지는 2016년 9월 발표, 2017년 1월 시행으로 알려져 있습니다. 확인 필요.
"Eight is great" 구호와 지점을 "stores"로 부른 관행은 Wells Fargo 연차보고서와 다수 보도에 나옵니다. 원문 표기 확인 필요.
2017년 이사회 보고서가 근본 원인을 판매 문화와 성과관리 체계로 지목하고, 경영진이 이를 개인 비위로 다뤘다고 지적한 부분은 요약입니다. 직접 인용하지 않았습니다. 표현을 보고서와 대조하세요.
연준 자산 상한은 2018년 부과. 2025년 해제로 보도되었으나 카드에는 부과 사실만 적었습니다. 게시 전 최신 상태를 확인하세요.
Meadows 문장은 직접 인용이 아닌 요지 정리입니다.

cards.title: Eight is great: how Wells Fargo's sales goals built a scandal
body: Wells Fargo called its bank branches "stores" and had a slogan for them: **"Eight is great."** The goal was eight products for every customer household: checking, savings, cards, loans.
For years, investors praised it as one of the best cross-sellers in banking. Then the numbers turned out to be partly fake.

image.label: A bank counter with a giant number 8 looming over the staff
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 은행 창구 뒤로 거대한 숫자 8이 그림자처럼 드리워져 있고, 직원들이 그 아래에서 서류를 급히 쌓는 모습. 실제 은행 로고, 역마차 상징, 브랜드 색상은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Great numbers, troubling reports.
body: It's the early 2010s. You lead a large retail bank. Branches track product sales every day, and results are strong.
But internal reports show some employees opening accounts customers never asked for, sometimes moving customers' money to fund them. What do you do?

options.text: Fire the employees who broke the rules and keep the sales goals
options.feedback: It's fast and shows you take rules seriously. But the pressure that produced the cheating stays, and new staff face the same targets.

options.text: Keep the goals, but add ethics training and a hotline
options.feedback: It signals that rules matter. But it asks people to resist the same pressure their pay and jobs depend on.

options.text: Drop product-count goals and judge branches on whether customers use what they open
options.feedback: You lose an impressive number and maybe some reported growth. In exchange, you stop rewarding the behavior you're trying to stop.

cards.title: The bank chose A. For years.
body: The goals stayed while the firings went on. The CEO stepped down weeks after the fines. A wider review in 2017 raised the estimate to as many as **3.5 million** accounts. In 2020, the bank agreed to pay $3 billion to settle federal investigations.

cards.title: Firing people didn't stop the loop.
body: Follow the pressure around the system:
list: High product goals create **pressure** in branches
Some staff hit goals by opening unwanted accounts
The numbers look great, so goals stay high
The pressure stays, and new staff feel it too
cards.callout: Each firing removed a person. The loop kept running and found the next one.
cards.softwareNote: A sales team paid on seats signed can push customers into seats they never use. The bookings look great until renewal, when the unused seats show up as churn.

cards.title: Structure drives behavior
body: When the same bad behavior shows up in many places, under many managers, the cause is usually the **structure**: the goals, pay and pressure people work inside. Systems thinker Donella Meadows made this point often. Swap the people, and the new ones tend to act the same way.
The board's own 2017 investigation reached a similar view. It traced the problem to the sales culture and the way performance was managed, and found leaders had treated it as individual misconduct.

cards.title: The good number was fast. The harm was slow.
body: Products per customer showed up in reports right away. The damage arrived later and somewhere else: unused accounts, surprise fees, complaints, unhappy staff.
A Los Angeles Times investigation described the branch pressure in 2013. The fines came about three years later. The bank dropped product sales goals for branch staff in early 2017.
Once product count became the target, it stopped telling leaders how strong customer relationships really were.

cards.title: Structure explains. It doesn't excuse.
body: People who broke the rules were still responsible for what they did. And not every bad act is a system problem. One person cheating may just be one person.
The signal is **spread**: the same act, in many places, under different managers. That's when to look at the system first.
Waiting has a price. Beyond the fines, the Federal Reserve capped the bank's growth in 2018, a limit that stayed in place for years.

cards.title: Now it's a heating and cooling company.
body: Your technicians earn a bonus for each add-on they sell: service plans, filters, upgraded parts. Add-on sales are up.
Now complaints arrive from three towns, about four different technicians: parts replaced that didn't need replacing. What do you do?

options.feedback: Quick and visible. But the bonus that tempted them still pays the next hire the same way.

options.text: Keep the bonus but cap it each month
options.feedback: A cap weakens the pull. But below the cap, you still pay for selling parts, not for fixing problems.

options.text: Pay for fixed jobs with few callbacks and good reviews, and spot-check replaced parts
options.feedback: Add-on sales may dip. But you now pay for what customers value, and spot-checks still catch anyone who cheats.

cards.title: When many people do the same wrong thing, look at what you reward.
body: One bad actor is a person problem. The same act in many places is a system problem, and firing people won't fix it.
**Try it today:** pick one target your team is measured on. Ask: what's the easiest way to hit it without helping a customer? If that path exists, someone is probably on it.
